cloze.text: Brand-name insulins used for Type I diabetes include Lantus®, Humalog® and {{c1::NovoLog®}}.
The first-line drug for Type I diabetes is {{c1::insulin}}; for Type II diabetes it is {{c2::metformin (Glucophage®)}}.
Dental relevance of Type I diabetes drugs (insulin): risk of {{c1::hypoglycemia}} if the appointment is long or insulin timing is off — {{c2::monitor vitals}}.
Dental relevance of Type II diabetes drugs: {{c1::xerostomia}}, increased {{c2::infection risk}}, delayed {{c3::healing}} and {{c4::periodontal diseases}}.
Common side effects of Type I diabetes drugs: {{c1::hypoglycemia}} and {{c2::weight gain}} (especially insulin).
Among Type II diabetes drugs, {{c1::GI upset}} is a typical side effect of metformin, and {{c2::hypoglycemia}} occurs especially with {{c3::sulfonylureas}}.
cloze.extra: Some Type II drugs also cause weight gain.

cloze.text: Type I diabetes is usually diagnosed {{c1::young}}, and {{c2::lifelong insulin}} is required.
Type II diabetes may be reversible/improved with {{c1::weight loss and a healthy lifestyle}}; it is often associated with {{c2::cardiovascular}} risk factors.
Diabetes is a disease in which blood {{c1::glucose}} levels are too high; sugar staying in the bloodstream instead of entering cells damages organs, blood vessels and {{c2::gums}}.
{{c1::Insulin}} is the hormone that helps sugar move from the blood into the cells.
In Type I diabetes the body's {{c1::immune system destroys the cells that make insulin}}, so insulin has to be {{c2::injected}}.
In Type II diabetes the body still makes insulin but cells don't respond properly, called {{c1::insulin resistance}}; it is usually linked to {{c2::obesity}}, inactivity and age.
The goal of diabetes treatment is to prevent complications by keeping blood sugar {{c1::stable throughout the day}}, especially {{c2::after eating}}.

{{c1::GLP-1 receptor agonists}} (e.g., Ozempic®, Wegovy®, Mounjaro®) mimic a natural hormone that increases insulin secretion, {{c2::slows gastric emptying}} and {{c3::suppresses appetite}}; used for Type 2 diabetes and weight loss.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "GLP = Gastric Lagging Progress" → GLP slows the stomach down = reflux builds up.

cloze.text: Levothyroxine is used for {{c1::hypothyroidism}}; methimazole and propylthiouracil (PTU) are used for {{c2::hyperthyroidism}}.
Levothyroxine replaces {{c1::T4}} (the inactive thyroid hormone), which the body converts to {{c2::T3}} (the active form).
Methimazole and PTU block thyroid hormone production by inhibiting {{c1::iodination}} in the thyroid gland.
Dental relevance of levothyroxine (hypothyroid patients): possible {{c1::delayed healing}} and increased {{c2::sensitivity to sedatives}} such as benzodiazepines.
Poorly controlled hyperthyroidism increases the risk of {{c1::thyroid storm}} (sudden fever, high heart rate, mental confusion); avoid {{c2::high-dose epinephrine}}.
A levothyroxine overdose causes weight loss, anxiety and palpitations — it {{c1::mimics hyperthyroidism}}.
Side effects of methimazole/PTU: skin rash, {{c1::agranulocytosis}} (dangerously low white blood cells) and {{c2::liver damage}} (especially with {{c3::PTU}}).
The thyroid produces T4 ({{c1::thyroxine}}) and T3 ({{c2::triiodothyronine}}).
{{c1::T4}} is the main hormone the thyroid makes but is less active; it is converted to {{c2::T3}}, the more active form, in organs like the {{c3::liver}}.
{{c1::T3}} is the thyroid hormone that regulates metabolism, heart rate and temperature.
Levothyroxine is synthetic {{c1::T4}}; it must be taken {{c2::on an empty stomach}} at the same time each day.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: the thyroid is the engine that controls body speed — too fast = hyperthyroidism, too slow = hypothyroidism.

cloze.text: Methimazole and PTU inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis and are used for hyperthyroidism and {{c1::Graves'}} disease.
{{c1::Iodine}} is necessary for thyroid hormone (T3, T4) production; deficiency can lead to {{c2::goiter}} (thyroid gland enlargement).
cloze.extra: Did you know: iodized salt was introduced as a simple way to prevent thyroid disorders.

cloze.text: Corticosteroids (also called {{c1::glucocorticoids}}) are synthetic drugs that mimic {{c2::cortisol}}, a hormone produced by the {{c3::adrenal cortex}}.
Corticosteroids treat asthma, allergic reactions, autoimmune diseases (e.g., lupus, rheumatoid arthritis) and {{c1::adrenal insufficiency}} ({{c2::Addison's}} disease).
Budesonide (brand {{c1::Pulmicort®}}) is a corticosteroid.
Corticosteroids work by suppressing inflammatory cells and signals (e.g., {{c1::prostaglandins}}, {{c2::cytokines}}), reducing pain, swelling and immune overreaction.
Corticosteroids can be taken orally, {{c1::topically}}, {{c2::inhaled}} or by injection, depending on the condition.

Corticosteroid side effects: xerostomia, delayed healing, increased infection risk, {{c1::peptic ulcers}} (take with food), bone loss ({{c2::osteoporosis}}) and {{c3::Cushingoid}} features like moon face or buffalo hump.
Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone) can cause {{c1::oral candidiasis}}; patients should {{c2::rinse thoroughly}} after use.
Immunosuppressants prevent {{c1::rejection of transplanted organs}} (e.g., kidney, liver, heart) and may be used for autoimmune conditions.
The immunosuppressant {{c1::cyclosporine}} (Sandimmune®) causes {{c2::gingival hyperplasia}} (overgrowth of gum tissue).
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Cyclosporine grows your 'cyclo-smile'" — gums growing too much and covering the teeth.

cloze.text: Statins inhibit {{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}} to reduce cholesterol synthesis in the {{c2::liver}}.
Main effect of statins: {{c1::↓}} LDL, {{c2::↑}} HDL, {{c3::↓}} triglycerides.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: LDL = "Low Desirable Lipid", HDL = "Highly Desirable Lipids".

cloze.text: Common statin side effects: {{c1::muscle pain (myalgia)}}, {{c2::liver enzyme elevation}} and GI upset.
{{c1::Grapefruit juice}} inhibits statin metabolism → increased statin toxicity.
Bile acid sequestrants (e.g., cholestyramine) bind {{c1::bile acids}} in the intestine, increasing {{c2::cholesterol excretion}}; main effect ↓ LDL.
Bile acid sequestrants cause {{c1::constipation}} and GI distress, and may interfere with {{c2::other drugs' absorption}}.
Niacin {{c1::reduces hepatic VLDL}}; fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) {{c2::activate lipoprotein lipase}}.
Main effect of niacin and fibrates: ↓ {{c1::triglycerides}}, mild ↑ HDL.
Side effects of niacin/fibrates: {{c1::flushing}} (niacin), {{c2::gallstones}} and liver toxicity.
Combining niacin with a {{c1::statin}} increases the risk of {{c2::myopathy}}.
Antihyperlipidemic agents lower blood lipids to reduce the risk of {{c1::atherosclerosis}} — fat building up inside blood vessels and narrowing them.
Lipid-lowering drugs lower {{c1::LDL}} (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol and triglycerides and can raise {{c2::HDL}} (high-density lipoprotein).
Grapefruit juice should be avoided with many lipid-lowering drugs, especially statins, because it interferes with {{c1::liver metabolism}} and may increase drug toxicity.
Short-acting beta-agonists (SABA) give {{c1::quick relief during an asthma attack}} — the "{{c2::rescue inhaler}}".
SABAs relax airway muscles within {{c1::minutes}}; LABAs relax airway muscles over {{c2::12 hours}}.
SABAs are inhaled as needed for immediate symptoms; ideally used no more than {{c1::2x/week}}.
SABA side effects: {{c1::tremor}}, {{c2::xerostomia}} and fast heartbeat.
Long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) {{c1::prevent attacks}}; they are taken daily for long-term control.
LABAs are inhaled {{c1::twice daily}} on schedule and are {{c2::never used for rescue}}.
LABA side effects: {{c1::throat irritation}} and headache.
LABAs must be used {{c1::with an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)}}, never alone.
Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) reduce airway inflammation for long-term control by suppressing the {{c1::immune response}} and inflammation.
Asthma ICS examples: fluticasone ({{c1::Flovent®}}) and mometasone ({{c2::Asmanex®}}).
ICS are inhaled once or twice daily {{c1::even if there are no symptoms}}.
ICS side effects: xerostomia and {{c1::oral candidiasis (thrush)}} — instruct the patient to {{c2::rinse the mouth}} after use.
Leukotriene modifiers prevent airway inflammation and mucus production by blocking {{c1::leukotrienes}}, which tighten airways and increase mucus.
Leukotriene modifiers are taken as a {{c1::once-daily pill}} as preventive therapy.
Leukotriene modifier side effects: headache and possible {{c1::mood changes}}; oral effects are {{c2::minimal}} (ask if asthma is well controlled).

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway condition in which the {{c1::bronchi}} become hypersensitive to triggers (allergens, exercise, cold air), causing {{c2::bronchoconstriction}}, inflammation and excess mucus.
cloze.extra: Did you know: the first inhaler (1956) was based on military aerosol technology.

cloze.text: Combination inhalers (e.g., {{c1::fluticasone + salmeterol}}) deliver anti-inflammatory and bronchodilating effects in one device, improving {{c2::adherence}}.

In the dental chair, asthma patients: watch for wheezing, shortness of breath or chest tightness; ask if she brought her {{c1::inhaler}}; consider {{c2::shorter appointments}} and a {{c3::semi-upright}} position.
Stress, anxiety and {{c1::sulfite preservatives}} in local anesthetics can trigger asthma; use {{c2::plain anesthetic}} when necessary.
In COPD, short-acting bronchodilators (SABA) give {{c1::emergency relief of acute symptoms}}; long-acting bronchodilators (LABA/LAMA) are {{c2::maintenance therapy}} to prevent symptoms long-term.
In COPD, inhaled corticosteroids are used to reduce inflammation in {{c1::moderate to severe}} COPD.
COPD SABA examples: albuterol (ProAir®, Ventolin®) and {{c1::levalbuterol}} (Xopenex®).
COPD long-acting bronchodilators: {{c1::formoterol}} (Foradil®, Perforomist®), arformoterol (Brovana®), {{c2::aclidinium}} (Tudorza®).
COPD inhaled corticosteroids: fluticasone (Flovent®) and {{c1::budesonide}} (Pulmicort®).
COPD inhaled corticosteroids have a {{c1::slow}} onset and are used consistently for long-term control.
COPD patients on SABAs may need to {{c1::use their inhaler before dental visits}}; watch for dry mouth.
COPD long-acting bronchodilators: risk of dry mouth; may require {{c1::chair adjustments}} to avoid {{c2::dizziness}}.
COPD inhaled corticosteroids can cause {{c1::oral candidiasis}} — advise rinsing the mouth thoroughly after use.
Side effect shared by all COPD inhaler classes (SABA, LABA/LAMA, ICS): {{c1::xerostomia}}.
cloze.extra: SABA: + headache, cough. LABA/LAMA: + dizziness, upset stomach, sore throat. ICS: + hoarseness, thrush, sore throat.

cloze.text: COPD inhaler side effects beyond xerostomia: SABA → headache and {{c1::cough}}; ICS → {{c2::hoarseness}}, thrush, sore throat.
COPD is a progressive lung disease that includes chronic {{c1::bronchitis}} and {{c2::emphysema}}; it causes airway inflammation, mucus buildup and destruction of {{c3::alveoli}}.
Common triggers of COPD exacerbation: {{c1::respiratory infections}}, allergens, air pollution and stress.

COPD treatment aims to reduce airway obstruction by relaxing bronchial muscles and reducing inflammation; COPD is {{c1::not reversible}}, but symptoms are managed with medications, lifestyle changes and {{c2::oxygen therapy}}.
Antacids directly {{c1::neutralize}} existing stomach acid by buffering {{c2::hydrochloric acid}}.
H2 blockers block {{c1::histamine (H2) receptors}} in the stomach lining, reducing acid secretion.
Proton pump inhibitors inhibit the {{c1::H⁺/K⁺ ATPase proton pump}} in {{c2::parietal cells}}, preventing the final step of acid production.
PPIs give long relief — up to {{c1::24}} hours, longer if used daily.
Antacid generics: calcium carbonate, {{c1::aluminum hydroxide}}, {{c2::magnesium hydroxide}}.
Antacid brands include {{c1::Tums®}}, Maalox® and Gaviscon®.
Ranitidine ({{c1::Zantac®}}), an H2 blocker, was withdrawn from the U.S. market in April 2020 because of {{c2::NDMA}} contamination, a potential carcinogen.
cloze.extra: Recalled in Canada from late 2019; Health Canada suspended all ranitidine products May 2020.

cloze.text: Antacid side effects: xerostomia, {{c1::constipation}} (aluminum), {{c2::diarrhea}} (magnesium), taste changes.
H2 blocker side effects: headache, dizziness, dry mouth and vitamin {{c1::B12}} malabsorption.
PPI side effects: headache, xerostomia, GI discomfort; long-term use → low {{c1::calcium}}, B12 and {{c2::iron}} absorption.
Laxative mechanisms vary: {{c1::bulk agents}} absorb water, {{c2::stimulants}} trigger motility, {{c3::softeners}} allow water into the stool.
Laxative generics: psyllium, {{c1::docusate sodium}}, {{c2::bisacodyl}}, mineral oil.
Chronic laxative use can alter {{c1::nutrient absorption}} and carries a risk of {{c2::hypokalemia}}.
Laxative overuse can lead to {{c1::dependency}} or electrolyte imbalance.
Antidiarrheals {{c1::reduce gut motility}} or promote reabsorption; some are {{c2::opioids}} or antispasmodics.
Antidiarrheal generics: {{c1::loperamide}}, {{c2::diphenoxylate + atropine}}, mebeverine.
Antidiarrheals: dental relevance {{c1::xerostomia}} or dehydration; they are often used {{c2::short-term}}, and loperamide is {{c3::OTC}}.
Antiemetics block neurotransmitters involved in nausea, e.g., {{c1::serotonin}}, dopamine and histamine.
Antiemetic generics: ondansetron, promethazine, {{c1::scopolamine}}, metoclopramide.
cloze.extra: Brands listed: Zofran®, Phenergan®, Dramamine®, Reglan®

cloze.text: Antiemetic brands include Zofran®, Phenergan®, {{c1::Dramamine®}} and Reglan®.
Antiemetics: dental relevance xerostomia, {{c1::sedation}} and taste changes; often used post-surgery, with {{c2::chemo}}, or for drug-induced nausea.
Appetite suppressants {{c1::mimic satiety hormones}} or affect CNS appetite pathways.
Appetite suppressant generics: {{c1::semaglutide}} (Ozempic®, Wegovy®), liraglutide, {{c2::phentermine-topiramate}}.
Appetite suppressants: dental relevance xerostomia, nausea and {{c1::altered gag reflex}}; GLP-1s double as {{c2::diabetes}} drugs.
Laxative misuse can lead to electrolyte imbalances like hypokalemia, especially in patients with {{c1::eating disorders}} or chronic constipation.
{{c1::Ondansetron}} (Zofran®) is commonly used for nausea post-anesthesia in dental settings, for patient comfort after sedation.

Local anesthetics block nerve impulse transmission by inhibiting the influx of {{c1::sodium}} ions through sodium channels; the action potential is not propagated because the {{c2::threshold}} level is never attained.
cloze.extra: Board Alert: the NBDHE will not ask injection-technique questions; it asks about the pharmacology of anesthetics (how they act, where they are metabolized, epinephrine, etc.).

cloze.text: Most local anesthetics are {{c1::vasodilators}}.
Epinephrine is added to local anesthetics for vasoconstriction: it {{c1::increases the duration}}, {{c2::reduces bleeding}} and decreases the potential for adverse reactions.
Local anesthetic solutions {{c1::decrease}} local tissue pH, creating a {{c2::burning}} sensation.
Adverse reactions to local anesthetics include {{c1::excitation}}, depression and {{c2::seizures}}.
A 1.8 mL cartridge of 1:50,000 epinephrine contains {{c1::0.036}} mg; of 1:200,000, {{c2::0.009}} mg.
"Cardiovascular patients" (epinephrine limit) include recent {{c1::myocardial infarction}}, angina, arrhythmias, severe or uncontrolled {{c2::hypertension}} and {{c3::congestive heart failure}}.
{{c1::Levonordefrin}} is a vasoconstrictor used only in {{c2::2% mepivacaine}} ({{c3::1:20,000}}).

{{c1::Sulfites}} are added as a preservative to local anesthetic cartridges that contain {{c2::epinephrine}}; anesthetics without epinephrine contain none, so they are safer for sulfite-sensitive patients.
cloze.extra: Sulfite-sensitive patients may have allergic-like reactions.

cloze.text: Ester local anesthetics: {{c1::procaine}}, tetracaine, {{c2::benzocaine}}.
Amide local anesthetics: lidocaine, {{c1::articaine}}, mepivacaine, {{c2::prilocaine}}, bupivacaine.
Name rule: esters have {{c1::one "i"}} (procaine); amides have {{c2::two "i"s}} (lidocaine).
Esters are mostly {{c1::topical}} anesthetics; amides are mostly {{c2::injectable}}.
cloze.extra: Clinical relevance: esters used topically (not injections); lidocaine is the main LA.

cloze.text: Esters are metabolized in the {{c1::plasma}} by {{c2::pseudocholinesterase}}; amides mainly in the {{c3::liver}} (hepatic enzymes), with some exceptions.
Esters are {{c1::unstable}} in solution; amides are {{c2::stable}}.
Allergic potential: {{c1::esters}} are more likely to cause allergic reactions; allergies to {{c2::amides}} are rare.
The main local anesthetic in dentistry is {{c1::lidocaine}}.
Mepivacaine comes as {{c1::3%}} plain and {{c2::2%}} with a vasoconstrictor.
cloze.extra: Book's table says "2% (with epi)"; the book's own bullet notes levonordefrin 1:20,000 is used only in 2% mepivacaine.

basic.front: Why may a patient on a GLP-1 drug (e.g., semaglutide) have a stronger gag reflex and tooth erosion?
basic.back: Delayed gastric emptying can indirectly trigger a gag reflex in the dental chair, and the resulting acid reflux can cause erosion.

basic.extra: Methimazole and propylthiouracil (PTU) are the anti-thyroid drugs in the book's table.
WakeUpMemory: Crestor sounds like CRISCO / CREAM STORE → lowers (bad) lipids.
WakeUpMemory: Questran → QUEST To RUN (to reduce bad fat).
SABA (rescue inhaler); also used in COPD (ProAir®, Ventolin®)

basic.front: Asthma patient on a SABA: what should you ask, and why?
basic.back: How often she uses it — frequent use = poorly controlled asthma.

basic.front: Why is nitrous oxide generally contraindicated in moderate to severe COPD (unlike asthma)?
basic.back: Risk of hypoxia or air trapping.

basic.front: Why can laxative overuse cause hypokalemia?
basic.back: Frequent bowel movements cause excessive loss of potassium through the stool.

basic.front: Why is epinephrine limited in cardiovascular patients?
basic.back: It is a vasoconstrictor and sympathomimetic that can overstimulate the heart (↑ heart rate, ↑ myocardial oxygen demand) → angina, arrhythmias or a cardiac event.

basic.front: Levonordefrin is used at 1:20,000 — a higher dose than epinephrine. Is it safer for cardiac patients?
basic.back: No. It is less potent than epinephrine, which is why the dosage appears higher, but it is not safer for cardiac patients.

mcq.question: A patient with Type I diabetes took her usual insulin but skipped breakfast. Ninety minutes into a long scaling appointment she becomes shaky, sweaty and confused. What is the most likely cause?
mcq.explanation: Insulin's main dental risk is hypoglycemia when the appointment is long or insulin timing is off (hence: monitor vitals). Hyperglycemia develops slowly and is not caused by the insulin dose.

mcq.question: A patient with poorly controlled hyperthyroidism needs local anesthesia. Which precaution is most important?
options: D. Use only ester topical anesthetics
mcq.explanation: Poorly controlled hyperthyroidism raises the risk of thyroid storm (fever, high heart rate, confusion), so high-dose epinephrine is avoided. Increased sedative sensitivity is a concern in HYPOthyroid patients on levothyroxine.

mcq.question: A patient taking atorvastatin reports new muscle aches. Which addition to her regimen most increases the risk of statin toxicity or myopathy?
mcq.explanation: Grapefruit juice inhibits statin metabolism (↑ toxicity) and niacin + statin ↑ myopathy risk. Cholestyramine may interfere with absorption of other drugs but does not raise statin toxicity.

mcq.question: Which lipid-lowering drug is most associated with flushing?
mcq.explanation: Flushing is the classic niacin side effect. Statins cause myalgia and liver enzyme elevation; bile acid sequestrants cause constipation/GI distress.

mcq.question: During scaling, a patient with asthma begins wheezing and is short of breath. Which of her inhalers should she use now?
mcq.explanation: Albuterol is a SABA — the rescue inhaler that relaxes airway muscles within minutes. Salmeterol is a LABA: it works over 12 hours and is never used for rescue.

mcq.question: A patient who uses a fluticasone inhaler has white, wipeable plaques on the palate. What is the best instruction?
options: B. Rinse the mouth thoroughly after each use
C. Use the inhaler only during attacks
D. Switch to a LABA alone
mcq.answer: B. Rinse the mouth thoroughly after each use
mcq.explanation: Inhaled corticosteroids cause oral candidiasis; rinsing after use prevents it. ICS must be taken daily even without symptoms, and LABAs are never used alone.

mcq.question: A patient with severe COPD is anxious about her appointment. Which statement is most accurate?
options: A. Nitrous oxide is the sedation of choice
B. Nitrous oxide is generally contraindicated because of hypoxia/air trapping risk
C. Her long-acting bronchodilator should be used for any acute attack
D. Inhaled corticosteroids give fast relief of acute symptoms
mcq.answer: B. Nitrous oxide is generally contraindicated because of hypoxia/air trapping risk
mcq.explanation: In moderate–severe COPD N2O risks hypoxia or air trapping. Long-acting bronchodilators are not for acute relief, and ICS have a slow onset.

mcq.question: A patient has taken omeprazole daily for years. Which long-term effect is most relevant?
options: B. Reduced calcium, B12 and iron absorption
mcq.answer: B. Reduced calcium, B12 and iron absorption
mcq.explanation: Long-term PPI use lowers calcium/B12/iron absorption. Diarrhea is a magnesium-antacid effect.

mcq.question: A patient with bulimia reports frequent laxative use. Which lab abnormality is she most at risk for?
mcq.explanation: Laxative misuse causes potassium loss in stool → hypokalemia, especially with eating disorders. Agranulocytosis is a methimazole/PTU effect.

mcq.question: A patient with a recent myocardial infarction needs anesthesia with 2% lidocaine 1:100,000 epinephrine. What is the maximum number of 1.8 mL cartridges?
mcq.explanation: Cardiac max epinephrine 0.04 mg ÷ 0.018 mg per 1:100,000 cartridge ≈ 2.2. 11.1 is the healthy-patient maximum (0.2 mg).

mcq.question: Which local anesthetic is metabolized mainly in the plasma by pseudocholinesterase and carries the highest allergic potential?
mcq.explanation: Benzocaine is an ester (one "i"): plasma pseudocholinesterase metabolism, higher allergy risk. The others are amides — liver metabolism, rare allergy.

mcq.question: A patient reports a sulfite sensitivity. Which anesthetic choice is most appropriate?
mcq.explanation: Sulfites are preservatives only in cartridges containing epinephrine (vasoconstrictor); plain anesthetics contain no sulfites.
